consensus_summary: All four consensus responses identify milk primarily as elementary spiritual teaching or basic nourishment of the Word suited to new or immature believers, contrasted with solid food/meat for the mature (1 Cor 3:1-2; Heb 5:12-14; 1 Pet 2:2). They note both a positive inflection (pure Word to be craved for growth) and a corrective one (remaining on milk signals stunted growth). Secondary senses include Promised Land abundance ('milk and honey'), free grace (Isa 55:1), maternal comfort, and poetic sweetness.
book_summary: The book defines milk as 'the word received' — teaching that another has already digested and that the learner swallows without personal work; the right first food of babes, given to grow them, but explicitly meant to be outgrown at weaning. It adds a distinctive mechanism: milk churned becomes butter (Prov 30:33; Isa 7:15), i.e., the received word worked toward solid food by the believer's own labor.
consensus_core_identification: Milk = elementary Christian doctrine / the pure nourishing Word, appropriate to spiritual infants and contrasted with solid food for the mature.
book_core_identification: Milk = the word received secondhand — teaching pre-digested by another and swallowed without the recipient's own work; proper first food for babes but designed to be outgrown, with churning (personal working of the word) producing butter as the transition toward solid food.
boundary_disagreement: The book sharpens the criterion distinguishing milk from meat: for the consensus, the difference is chiefly content-level (elementary vs. advanced doctrine); for the book, it is the mode of reception (digested by another vs. worked by oneself). The book also unambiguously fixes milk's telos as something to be outgrown at weaning (leaning on Isa 28:9), whereas the consensus holds the positive 1 Peter craving-sense and the corrective Paul/Hebrews sense in complementary tension. Additionally the book introduces butter as a named intermediate stage (Prov 30:33; Isa 7:15) absent from all consensus responses, and silently drops the OT abundance ('milk and honey') sense from the entry, though that omission concerns a separate sense rather than a contradiction.
rationale: The book's central referent is the same as the consensus's: milk is elementary teaching/the Word as first food for spiritual babes, contrasted with solid food for the mature, citing the very same anchor texts (1 Pet 2:2; 1 Cor 3:1-2; Heb 5:12-13). This rules out DIVERGENT and NOVEL. But the book does more than reword: it materially refines the definition by specifying that milk is teaching pre-digested by another and 'swallowed without work,' making recipient labor rather than doctrinal difficulty the boundary condition, and it adds the churning-to-butter mechanism as the process of maturation. These are real precision changes at the boundary of the category, so REFINED rather than MATCH.
strongest_objection: One could argue for MATCH: the book's 'pre-digested teaching' and the butter mechanism could be read as vivid elaboration of the same consensus identification (elementary Word for babes vs. solid food for the mature) with identical proof-texts, and the churning detail as immaterial color rather than a boundary change. Conversely, the 'swallowed without work' criterion is an interpretive gloss not directly stated in any cited verse — Prov 30:33 concerns wrath and strife, and its symbolic transfer to word-maturation is a creative inference, which is why citation support is only partial.
